## Solution

**Claim:** $X_1 = X_2$ need **not** hold. The given equality constrains only the "diagonal blocks" of $X_1$ and $X_2$ with respect to the range of $P$; the "off-diagonal blocks" are free. A counterexample suffices.

**Counterexample.**

Let $H = \mathbb{C}^2$ and let $P$ be the orthogonal projection onto the first coordinate:
$$
P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 1-P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Set
$$
X_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad X_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Clearly $X_1, X_2 \in B(H)$ and $X_1 \neq X_2$.

Compute the left-hand side with $X_1$:
$$
PX_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\quad
PX_1P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
$$
(1-P)X_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\quad
(1-P)X_1(1-P) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Hence
$$
PX_1P + (1-P)X_1(1-P) = 0.
$$

For $X_2 = 0$, trivially
$$
PX_2P + (1-P)X_2(1-P) = 0.
$$

Therefore
$$
PX_1P + (1-P)X_1(1-P) = PX_2P + (1-P)X_2(1-P),
$$
yet $X_1 \neq X_2$.

**Why this happens (structural reason).** With respect to the decomposition $H = \operatorname{ran}P \oplus \ker P$, every operator decomposes into a $2\times 2$ block matrix
$$
X = \begin{pmatrix} PXP & PX(1-P) \\ (1-P)XP & (1-P)X(1-P) \end{pmatrix}.
$$
The expression $PXP + (1-P)X(1-P)$ retains only the two diagonal blocks and discards the off-diagonal blocks $PX(1-P)$ and $(1-P)XP$. Thus two operators agree under this map precisely when they share the same diagonal blocks; their off-diagonal blocks may differ arbitrarily. In the counterexample above, $X_1$ has a nonzero off-diagonal block $PX_1(1-P) = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ while $X_2$ has all blocks zero, yet both have identical (zero) diagonal blocks.

**Conclusion.** The implication is **false** in general; $X_1 = X_2$ does not follow from the stated equality.

### PROOF COMPLETE
